segments.text: Hello and welcome to the Planetary Regeneration Podcast. I'm your host, Greg Rielandwe.
All right. Well, today I am joined by Victoria Lures and I'm really excited to chat with you, Victoria, about your...
I mean, probably this conversation will go much broader than the recent book that you've published, Church of the Wild, is my guess.
But sort of starting with that is a foundation for the conversation and just digging in. And I know my listeners will probably be pretty interested.

There's a... I think a very vibrant conversation at the moment about a lot of the... I don't know. I guess I would say functional, economic, social elements of regeneration and what it means to reconnect human society to a thriving planet.

And in this case, I think that this is an opportunity for us to talk a little bit more about the spiritual side and the mystical side and the side that's harder to explain or maybe capture into language.
And so, yeah, I'm excited to dig in with you and thanks so much for joining us.
Yeah. Thank you for finding me.
Yeah. Do you want to just start with maybe just a brief introduction to yourself and maybe a little bit about the adventure that you're on right now?
Your nomadic adventure at the moment seems like there's probably some very juicy stuff to pull out there.
Yeah, sounds good. Well, I'm excited to meet you and to be introduced to your community and just looking through your website a bit.
These are the kinds of conversations, these multidisciplinary conversations that are needed right now.
It is not any one of these areas, these disciplines, but it's all of them.
And as we sort of on the left tend to diminish the others that aren't what we believe is the central focus.
We diminish the whole movement and so I love that you're bringing in all the different voices and specialties that are needed.
So thank you for your commitment and work.
Let's see how to tell us very quickly.
I call myself a wild church pastor, although I think I'm probably a little bit more right now.
Maybe a wild church apostle because I'm not leading a local wild church right now.
I'm in the midst of a year long, as you mentioned, at least a year of nomadic life, of kind of just going where I'm called, literally called to do a workshop or something like that.
And now that it's sort of post-ish pandemic and people are gathering together again, I've been doing a lot of different workshops in different places.
And so I just have surrendered to that invitation and spending this next year, at least working on my next book, which is about how to belong to place when place doesn't belong to you.

And so that's not only for somebody like me who's nomatically traveling around and not belonging, you know, living in one place, but also to all of us, because it's not really true that a place belongs to us.
What is, how do we change that paradigm even if we own property to shift that around that the plate that we belong to this place and this planet.
So I'm interested in that that has economic and social and functional elements, but is also very much a spiritual issue.
I was a pastor within, you know, sort of traditional independent churches for on and off for about 25 years.
And I took a long seven year break in the middle of that and led a youth's climate nonprofit with my son starting from when he was 12 till he was about 18.
And then kind of came back into the church for a little bit knowing that the burnout I experienced in the church was not dissimilar to the burnout I experienced within the environmental movement.
And in that place of like just confusion and emptiness with when I turned to the land herself, you know, just like spent hours under this huge oak tree where I lived in Southern California.

And in that place and in a workshop that I did a 5D intensive I did with Bill Plotkin, I know I know you've had on your show before looking at our shadow side, but doing that inner inner work in relationship with with the land herself, brought about a transformation within myself and within the other participants.

And Bill Plotkin was pretty insistent that his work is not spiritual. I think he might say it's all connected psychospiritual work, but he was like, this is not spiritual work, this is depth psychology.

But it absolutely is, it's very spiritual work. And after that five days in that place of like nothing is, you know, burnout when I went to that first program about seven years ago is when it started to come together for me.

That these are not separate that this deep connection with the sacred that I had been experiencing my whole life in relationship with the natural world and my connection with the sacred that I found in in the church tempered then by abuses within human community within the church, which has become complicit with empire throughout the centuries.

But finding that these are not separate and we in our culture and definitely in the church separates them that our spirituality is one thing and our connection with nature and taking care of the planet is another thing.

Even though 30 years ago I did work to help the conservative evangelical right to see that caring for creation was part of their own tradition and legacy and heritage and was not a political agenda at all.

And it was it was pretty successful to sent out to 50,000 evangelical churches, you know, well, with that 30 years ago, but we've become more and more polarized since then. So that separation between our core spiritual life and the rest of the natural world is deeply embedded in our culture and in our religions and and it's shifting.

It's starting to change, but it's that that third way that reconnected way reconnecting our spirituality, our lifestyle, our way of being in intimate relationship with the more than human others that are in our home place became the core piece for me that brought me out of that place of burnout and into a new way of practicing.

Practicing religion, honestly, not just spirituality, but religion, religion actually means reconnection, legios, it's really gios is the Latin word and legios is like a ligament that means reconnection.
And so human beings have always had religion because we tend, I think, to disconnect to exile the exile and return is like a rhythm, a pattern of being human.

And so we need spiritual practices to reconnect with the natural world, to reconnect with one another. And so that's when I started the church of the wild, which was a practice of being in community and bringing creating and adapting to the world.

And then I started to be doing spiritual practices to reconnect with the natural world as sacred is really the whole point of it. And after I did that, I started to meet other spiritual leaders who are doing the same thing with different influences and realize that this is a work of, this is a larger story, a larger story of spirit as well as earth herself calling people into relationship once again.

And so then started their wild church network and there's over 2000 different communities that are starting up in North America mostly. And then also about seven years ago started seminary of the wild for people to go deeper into this work and to their calling as a leader to reconnect people in their spiritual lives and the rest of natural world.

And it's now a seminary of the wild is now called center for wild spirituality. It's a broader it's broader than within the Christian religion. There's a lot of probably half the people that come through our programs aren't connected with Christianity and in fact those edges between us versus them, these different kinds of denominations are important for identity, I suppose, but I think what the age that we're entering into those edges are dissolving.

And so it's important to emphasize that this isn't about a particular religion, it's about connecting with the sacred directly through the more than human others who are our teachers and preachers and co congregants in in practicing reconnection religion.

Yeah, that's all really interesting. I mean, there's a few different things that sprung up as you were telling that little arc of just your work and some of my questions, I guess, are maybe just to probing curiosity of in order to learn just from where you're sitting with your experience and sort of having started out as a pastor and having started out within the church.

How would you delineate or differentiate between religious and spiritual in the way that you use those two words to start? And I don't want to go too deep into all of that world, but I'm just really curious because I think that's a good conversational foundation.

I think so. I think within the last three years, you know, Pew does a study every year of the religious practices of Americans. And up until three years ago, the top, you know, it used to be the Roman Catholics were the top affiliation for Americans.

And then it's been evangelicals for a while. And a few years ago, I think it's about three years ago, spiritual but not religious is the top religious group in America right now. And I think I would have affiliated more with spiritual but not religious. And I think the way that's meant is like we're tired of the religious trappings of control of telling us what what God means, what it means to be in relationship with God.

I mean, patriarchal, it's racist, it's control, it's, you know, all of those things are real. And so I think people are wanting to distance from that. So spiritual but not religious meant, you know, I have a relationship with sacred. It's my own way. I don't listen to the institutions of patriarchy essentially.

And so I would identify that way. But once I understood what religion actually means, I'm sort of re-embracing it and redefining it just as I redefine, just as the work of church of the wild, like just putting wild with church kind of redefines it. Even if you're not somebody who's drawn to church, it's sort of interesting to see, oh, what is church of the wild, not in the wild, not just in the wild, but of the wild.

What does that actually mean? It arouses a curiosity. And I'm feeling that way about the word religion now that to be spiritual is sort of like your own personal way of being in the world. And religion is a way of reconnecting with one another with your community, with the land.
So I guess I'm redefining it for myself and starting to talk about that. But I think that most people see religion as connected with the institution.
Right. It seems like religion has connotations of ritual and community and maybe commitment to a liturgy or maybe some sort of dogma.
Right. It's the dogma and the control and those kinds of things that we're wanting to transcend.
But the things we want to still hold on to are the ritual, is the community, is the sense of belonging, is the sense of shared values.
So there are some things that are worth holding on to and there are some things worth very much worth letting go of.

So I think we can redefine religion, but in general, when you use the word religion in our culture, it has a lot of that, you know, reality of institutional collusion with colonization and empire and control and dogma.

But it doesn't, that's not what it's about. That's not what it's meant to be. It's like what humans do. What we do. It's what we do with things. We scoot up. And we, and we come back again, you know, we do that as as individual humans, right?
Like we aren't perfect. We mess up. We hurt people. And it's the coming back together. It's the ongoing conversation that, that keeps us in relationship, that is how we evolve and grow.
And that's what love is. Love is that making mistakes and allowing that and working them out and forgiving and starting again.

And so to have that kind of relationship with one another and with the land, you know, because we can get stuck feeling the pain of the damage that we're that we're dealing with right now in our culture.

And it can make us feel frozen and until we can, you know, sort of like not just reckon with it, but really do the deeper work of looking at it, seeing it, making a man's forgiveness and entering in in a new way, that's the way through.
So we do have some things to learn from traditional religions to include those pieces and transcend the others.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, interesting. You were mentioning that there's about 2000 or more communities that are sort of coming together and exploring this in this wild church network.
And what would one expect if, you know, if a listener was like, oh, this is interesting. I kind of want to connect with with a local community and just go see or participate or share.

What is it like? Like what do people? I'm sure there's a close spectrum of expressions, but what's the, you know, maybe what are some of the patterns and what are people, what is working in this balance as people are exploring what to keep and what sort of rituals or ceremonies or ways of engaging are making sense and what are things that maybe are being left behind.

Are there patterns there that you're starting to see? Yeah, it's exactly. It's a perfectly worded question, actually, because it's really just observing what's emerging. And we don't in the network. We don't say, here's how you do it. Here's the one, two, three, because it's very particular to place. It's very particular to who the, who the person is who feels that they just need to start this.

Most people are saying, I just need to do this for me, if anybody else comes, great. So that's true, whether they're a pastor and they start of a traditional church and they start a community of their own on the side. They don't even, a lot of them don't even try to bring their church community along because they know it's something they need that where they're, they need for themselves to have that kind of practice and community.

There are, of course, then many ways of living this out. Some communities are more activists, you know, and they're involved in local activism, ecological protection. Some communities do, you know, are involved with a land trust and do that kind of work or they'll do community gardens, you know, so they're very active.
Some communities are very contemplative and they go into the forest and they silently listen, you know, for most of the time. It's like a quicker forest meeting or something.

I would say the one piece, there's a few pieces that I have observed are common. One is they meet outside. They're not inside of buildings, but that can be anywhere from, you know, outside the city limits on a off of a hiking trail.
It could be a city park. It could be a parking lot, you know, where there was one in Vancouver I went to, where the crows roosted. And so we met in a Costco parking lot.
And the crows came in in the hundreds and just spending the time paying attention and listening to them. But the, I think, so that's, that's common.
And another piece is this practice of wandering, which is a core practice that Bill, that Bill Pluckin uses in Annas Valley Institute work.
It's a core piece that the nature and forest therapy guides, you know, forest bathing folks utilize. It's a common practice of slowing down and entering into relationship.
So it's not just slowing down in order to, you know, feel relaxed and enjoy the pretty trees and the beautiful sunset or something. That's part of it.
But the part of it that is church of the wild is that we are entering into back into full relationship.

We are remembering that we are part of nature. We are remembering ourselves again, remembering ourselves again back into the larger beloved community that goes beyond our species that we're not used to.

And so that takes practices of reality of remembering that we are not only in physical community, that the air that we're breathing and the water we drink, the food we eat are all shared by the others on the planet.

But we are also emotionally connected and we're spiritually connected. And we as a culture have forgotten that and forgotten how to even have conversations beyond not just beyond our species, but even beyond our own little, you know, circles.
Like we've become so polarized as humans that it's difficult to have a conversation with somebody on, you know, another end of a spectrum of you.
And then multiply that when you go outside of your species. But we have it within us. We have the capacity to engage with the more than human others in a way that is spiritually real.

And so, you know, our indigenous brothers and sisters never lost the capacity to do that. And all of us come from some, you know, if you go back enough, ancestral, the generations, you'll see that all of our ancestors had deep, earth-based spiritual relationships with their place.
They were disconnected systemically by colonization and, you know, empire because you can't take over a land of people that you can disconnect them from the land.
And so just othering the land became part of our Western culture. And so we need to learn these practices again.
So the centerpiece practice of that is this wandering. So we'll gather, you know, all the, there's a lot of wild churches have a similar framework as what I'm going to say right now.
So we'll gather in a circle somewhere outside. Some places have drumming, some places have music, some singing, some places have extended silence of just listening and remembering where you are.

Some places look to all the directions to bless and honor all of the beings and all directions. And then there's an invitation leads to an invitation to go out beyond the circle and wander individually.

To use John Muir's word, sonter, to sonter slowly, to walk reverently among these others. And in this place, and allow yourself to be drawn to a particular other, a particular, you know, place, a little place along the shoreline, a grasshopper, you know, whatever it is.

And just to linger there and to listen and, you know, maybe bring your journal and see what poem comes through you. Maybe enter into conversation of, you know, I love the Mary Oliver poem, a wild geese in the middle of it. She says, tell me of despair yours. And I'll tell you mine.

Just sharing, you know, what's burdening you and really listening to these others as separate sacred beings, seeing what emerges for you. And, you know, often people go out and they'll feel drawn to a tree or something and they'll sit there and a connection that they don't really have words for.

And they'll come back to the circle then everybody comes back after, you know, 45 minutes, maybe an hour comes back in the circle and shares their experience. And that's the church service. You know, it's like we're learning to listen again. We're learning to be in conversation. We're learning to honor each other's experience of the sacred.

And, and to name it for what it is to name that you're you're in this, you have this opportunity to sit underneath a, you know, an ancient oak tree and you have memories or thoughts that come up as you're as you're there and paying attention with all of your senses.
And you can feel emotions and some of those are your own emotions. Some of them might be something you're feeling from the land. Some of them might be the feelings mediated by the sacred presence.

You know, it's like it's there's no dogma about it. Like it's just being open to what emerges and sharing that with others. Sort of like when you share a dream with somebody like you can you can have a dream and you thought, that's interesting. Maybe it means this or that.

But when you share it with other people and they get and you get their curiosities and they're noticing different things, then it comes alive for you more and it's something you can really become some psychic material you can you can work with.

And if you bring it and so it's just like creating these relationships and as we create these relationships, we actually are opening our shelves up to falling in love to falling in love with your place to falling in love with particular places because we fall in love with the particular.

You can't just love the whole earth because it's too big. You know, you fall in love with particular other beings and other places. And as you fall in love, a relationship happens and then you're committed, you identify then with this place and you're committed to protecting it.
And then it's based on relationship not just on a sense of morality of what's right and wrong and we're all going to die if we don't do this, which isn't untrue.
But it's not appealing then to people's fears. It's appealing to the fact that we care about these others and we're in kindred relationship with them.

And as long as we're not in kindred relationship, then it's a constant fight of campaigning of trying to change things because it's the right thing to do or because it's the political way to a better way of living or something.
But it's then just based on relationship. It's like, I love this place. I love this particular tree out here. I have a relationship with this deer that comes to my house every day.
It just changes the way you are in the world, which is kind of the point of church, right?
It's not just about going and enjoying some nice music and a good saying, hide your friends. It's like, it's about we need support as we change our value system.
The value system is the thing that needs to change in order for all of these other economic and technological and energy-based things to happen.
They do have a spiritual foundation. So this is about creating practices to make that shift.

Yeah, that makes sense. I'm curious about your perspective about the relationship between, I guess, this new maybe decentralized religion approach where people are taking responsibility for their own experience and grounding that in a specific place and context and politics.

The relationship between, because as you noted, I mean, I think religion has a very long history, not just in the West, in many cultures of a deep connection with the political or the structures of power.

There's probably many reasons for that. And as you were mentioning, that's probably the reaction to that is probably a big part of the spiritual not religious, the new denomination of spiritual and not religious.
But I'm curious, what is the relationship from your perspective? Because also in the course of the conversation you mentioned sort of like we the left.
So I get the sense that you have some political sensibilities and obviously like worked for a period of time with your son on climate.
And that's essentially a political act. So I'm just curious, what's a healthy relationship between the political and the religious in this moment in history?

So that's one question. I'm also really curious just about if this is resonating across political boundaries, you know, in this time of polarization or do you feel like it's particularly resonating sort of only within certain communities that already sort of have their mind made up.
Probably, you know, I do see there are there are some communities, some wild church communities who are from the evangelical or Baptist or sort of more conservative political communities.
They're going to have a little more, a lot more resistance if they're trying to stay connected with their, with the institutional church because it's all been politicized.

You know, these issues have been politicized. So caring about the land has been politicized within conservative churches and resistance to that becomes resistance to, you know, a political ideology on the left.
So there are definitely, there's definitely more people who would probably politically align with the left within this movement. That is true.
I think it has the capacity to, to breach that because the one thing we do have in common is that we live here, you know, we live on this land.

I have, I have hope that that the land and survival within the growing climate crises will give us those opportunities to have more conversations across this polarity and find that literal common ground that becomes a common ground for, for conversation beyond just sort of spouting.
I think that the other part of your question is what could a healthy connection between our political selves and our religious selves? What could that look like?
And I think that the role that connecting with the land plays is essential in, in that more healthy relationship.

Because one of the things is we need to learn how to trust our own inner authority, you know, like that having this meme conversation that's not really even a conversation of just spouting ideologies back and forth, that's not a conversation.

You know, in order to deepen beyond that, you have to be in touch with your own inner authority. So there's everything is not defined by external authorities and Empire House and agenda of disconnecting us from that inner authority because that leads to trouble, right, to the dominant culture.

And so I think a political response to this intimacy of our place is essential. You can't really disconnect it. And if you do, it becomes just sort of like a, you know, spiritual bypass even of like is in this land beautiful.
Oh, yeah, well, it's being deforested tomorrow. And I just don't have the time to do anything about it. You know, I mean, it just it ought to it, it necessarily is interconnected.

But if it's interconnected in a way that's birthed out of relationship, relationship with the community, relationship with the complex communal issues, as well as the relationship with the more than human community, that there are more values here than what's best for the humans.

You know, how is this best also for the land and the waters not just because we need the land and the waters to survive, but because they have inherent value, which I think is inherently a religious issue.
The the personhood of the sacred reality of all things is included in almost every religion.
But it's overlooked when we get into issues of, you know, human thriving and particular human that thrive and the others that are not as important, which is what we do in our culture.
So, you know, how we engage politically can be influenced by our is influenced by our spiritual and religious reality.
And so, as long as we keep it in that place of, you know, just just following the external authorities who are not necessarily the ones to be trusted, that keeps us in a in a place of powerlessness.

So, I think, I think, you know, one of the things I'm doing when I'm going to Scotland tomorrow is talking with some of the people in the, in the Hebrides Islands, who have engaged in some very powerful political activism that has had meaningful change has happened.

And it's based in the first step is having people is is helping people to reconnect with their place as sacred to reconnect with their place in an intimate way of remembering stories, remembering writing new songs, you know, like really falling in love again.
And out of that, then comes energy to be engaged in political activism that protects the place from usually corporate or usually corporate abuse.
And so, that takes more than just like the constant raising money and trying to get people to sign things and whatever like like because you should do this.

It's like we're so mobile too in this country that it's hard to, it's hard to do that. But how do we reconnect people how to fall in love with their place again to know that they belong to a larger story.

And in that, then you're not just like doing a political action or going out and voting because you should, but it's like you're protecting your kin, you know, these, you're protecting like your own daughter and you do it because you care and you're in love.
And so it just feels like they're they're intimately connected, but in a very different way.
Yeah, yeah, definitely sort of a side note. Have you come across the story of place, the regentist's groups, the story of place.
I've heard it, but I'd love to hear more about it.
Well, I mean, it's a really awesome group of humans based out of, I mean, members of regentists live all over, but I think they're based out of Santa Fe.
Story of place was developed in order to reconnect communities and bring them together to regenerate a story of place.
And so they're doing sort of deep geological history of the place and their and cultural history of the place.

And over the course of their process, sort of the essence of the place is revealed, just like you could tune into the essence of a human like everyone is unique and everybody has some sort of unique thing that it's not just personality.
It's not the superficial stuff. It's something that's more core to that.
And they use it as a part of their, you know, that it's a sort of design and architecture group.

At the end of the day, they're using it to work with municipalities or groups to start to re anchor design decisions about a community in, you know, into the authority of the community and the place instead of kind of imposing some external ideal of what how things should work or why they should work some way.

But actually to sort of source it from the place instead.
